summary:
Emergency Ordinance No. 89/2001, adopted 21 June 2001 and in force 26 June 2001, repealed Penal Code Article 200 and decriminalised consensual adult same-sex relations; Articles 197, 198, 201 and 202 were redefined in gender-neutral terms applying equally to sexual acts with persons of different or same sex. Pending investigations, trials and custodial sentences under former Article 200(2)–(4) were preserved only where the facts remained punishable under other provisions, with reclassification by the execution court. Same-sex relations are legal nationwide.

Government Ordinance 137/2000 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sex and sexual orientation, and a 2000 law extends that prohibition across employment, goods and services, housing, education, health care, audiovisual programming, justice, public services and social security, enforced by the National Council for Combating Discrimination (CNCD). Outright International records that institutional follow-through on this protection is limited. The CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials during 2023.

The Penal Code was amended in 2006 to add incitement to discrimination, homophobic bias as an aggravating circumstance permitting higher sentences, and incitement to hatred and harassment on sexual-orientation grounds. These provisions are framed on sexual orientation and do not expressly cover gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics; ILGA-Europe's rainbow map records for 2025 that hate-crime and hate-speech protections lack express coverage of those grounds, and the application of the 2006 provisions is described as difficult to assess or not yet applied.

Legal gender recognition exists and is court-based. Since 1996 a person who has undergone sex reassignment surgery has been able to change sex in official documents, but the governing law is vague and incomplete, producing inconsistent judicial practice in which some authorities have refused recognition unless a surgical intervention had occurred. A change of civil status requires a court decision based in practice on a certificate from the Institutul Național de Medicină Legală (INML) issued through an intrusive and ad hoc procedure. The difficulty of that procedure frequently prevents documents reflecting gender identity from being obtained, which in turn creates problems in accessing health care, transport passes and banking services. ILGA-Europe's rainbow map records that during January–December 2025 Romania had no fair, transparent, self-determination-based framework free from abusive requirements, and no non-binary option.

In October 2024 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Romania had infringed a transgender man's rights in the Mirzarafie-Ahi case, which concerns recognition in Romania of a UK gender recognition certificate, and held that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition. On 31 March 2026 the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity; the ruling became definitive when the Bucharest Tribunal rejected appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates. ACCEPT Romania, announcing the outcome on Trans Day of Visibility, urged others who had changed their documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania.

Marriage is limited to a union between a man and a woman under Civil Code Article 259 and implementing legislation, and no civil-partnership regime exists. The 2018 referendum to amend the constitution to ban same-sex marriage failed on low turnout, same-sex marriage and civil-partnership bills were rejected in 2013–2015, and the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017. The European Court of Human Rights ruled on 23 May 2023 that a failure to allow marriage or partnership breaches Article 8, and the Prime Minister stated in November 2023 that Romania will not legalise either. In Coman and Others in June 2018 the Court of Justice of the European Union held that same-sex spouses married in an EU country have residence rights, and Romania's highest courts ruled the same year for equivalent residency and legal rights.

Anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the 2025 presidential campaign. Candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February 2025, Prime Minister Marcel Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes and in October 2025 opposed amendments to identity documents for legal gender recognition as creating confusion and eroding traditional norms, and in the same month political figures claimed children could choose their gender without parental consent. A Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements. ACCEPT Romania's chapter in the ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report states that eight of nine country submissions reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people, and cites the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.

Regulatory follow-up did occur. After B1 TV's News Pass programme on 5 June 2025 framed Pride as a provocation with derogatory portrayals of LGBTI visibility, the National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to the channel in August 2025 for breach of the Audiovisual Code prohibition on generalised defamatory statements against groups defined by sexual orientation, following an ACCEPT complaint.

Pride events proceeded in 2025 amid documented hostility. The Bucharest Pride march on 7 June 2025 drew approximately 31,000 people demanding simplified legal gender recognition procedures, civil-union legislation and protection against hate speech and prejudice-based crimes; AP reported the 20th anniversary march in June 2025 as drawing tens of thousands. In July 2025 Oradea Pride went ahead despite a third-year municipal ban attempt, under heavy police supervision, with nine organisers and participants fined and a subsequent application to the European Court of Human Rights; Pride events in Cluj-Napoca, Brașov, Timișoara and Iași took place without incidents.

Attempts to legislate against gender identity and homosexuality have so far been blocked or stripped. A June 2020 parliamentary amendment imposing a blanket ban on gender identity studies without public debate was struck down by the Constitutional Court in December 2020; the anti-LGBTQ provisions of April 2022 Senate bills banning 'gay propaganda' in schools and discussion of homosexuality and gender identity in public spaces were removed from the final version; and anti-discrimination provisions in March 2024 education-law drafts drew protests from 13 religious groups and a counter-response from more than 50 organisations. LGBTI organisations can register and operate, and in October 2025 three training-of-trainers sessions were held for police officers, prosecutors and social workers to recognise, investigate and respond to hate crimes targeting LGBTI people.
tangentialFactors:
A Council of Europe thematic review published in January 2023, 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania', is a national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 covering legal and policy frameworks, applicable European Court of Human Rights case-law and international standards. In 2021 the same court found violations of Articles 8 and 11 for the failure to investigate effectively the 20 February 2013 homophobic disruption of an LGBTQ film screening, finding discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds.

Survey evidence in the inventory concerns sexual orientation and LGBTI identity generally and contains no separate transgender-specific tolerance or victimisation figure beyond a general statement that attitudes in Romania are conservative regarding the rights of gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender citizens. A 2019 poll of about 3,200 people found 53% of LGBTI people were '(Almost) never open' about being LGBTI; an ACCEPT 2010 survey reported 68.2% had suffered discrimination or exclusion on grounds of sexual orientation or identity, most often on streets at 49.5%; and a 2013 Fundamental Rights Agency survey ranked Romania third of the surveyed jurisdictions after Croatia and Bulgaria, with 21% reporting attack or threat of violence in the previous five years.

Men who have sex with men remain barred from blood donation under a rule found to be illegal sexual-orientation discrimination in September 2007; a January 2008 Health Ministry removal of the ban is recorded as not yet implemented. A FRA-commissioned legal study of February 2008 by Romanița Elena Iordache and Iustina Ionescu maps how Romanian law implemented the EU Employment Directive 2000/78/EC and free-movement rules for LGBT partners, including national anti-discrimination concepts, CNCD enforcement powers and NGO complaints, and serves as a dated baseline for the country's protection architecture. IPSOS PRIDE 2023 found 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking legal gender recognition must obtain a court decision supported in practice by an INML certificate issued through a procedure developed ad hoc to fill a legal vacuum; because the governing statute is vague, outcomes vary by court and some authorities have required evidence of a sex-reassignment intervention. Without updated documents, residents face documented difficulty obtaining health care, transport passes and banking services.

Discrimination complaints on grounds of sex or sexual orientation fall to the CNCD, which has investigation and fining powers; it has acted against employers and service providers, including a 2005 fine against TAROM for refusing same-sex partners couples discounts, and investigated printing houses that refused LGBT and gender-equality materials in 2023. Hate-crime aggravation and incitement provisions added to the Penal Code in 2006 rest on sexual-orientation grounds rather than gender identity, and their practical application is described as difficult to assess or not yet applied.

Open homosexuality remains uncommon outside major urban centres, with rural LGBTI Romanians typically remaining closeted; visible communities and annual pride parades exist in Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca, Iași and Timișoara. A 2019 poll found 53% of LGBTI respondents were almost never open about their identity. LGBTI organisations are able to register and operate, and ACCEPT Romania advises residents who changed documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania following the March 2026 definitive judgment.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no trans-specific homicide or violence figure for Romania with a denominator, so no comparison between trans-targeted violence and the general homicide rate can be stated; the survey data cited above measures self-reported LGBTI experience without a transgender breakdown.

Whether the March 2026 definitive judgment in the Mirzarafie-Ahi case has changed routine practice for legal gender recognition beyond transcription of certificates issued in other EU countries is not sourced. Whether the INML certificate procedure has been reformed, and whether the intrusive requirements described in the source have been replaced, remain unresolved in the inventory.

The outcome of the application to the European Court of Human Rights following the July 2025 Oradea Pride fines is not sourced. Whether the January 2008 Health Ministry removal of the blood-donation ban for men who have sex with men was ever implemented is recorded as not implemented as of the source's account and remains unresolved here.

Whether the hate-crime and hate-speech provisions added in 2006 have been applied in any prosecuted case is described in the source as difficult to assess or not yet applied; no case-level confirmation appears in the inventory.
